subject: Credits vs Flex Commit — quantization playbook for pilot
messages:
From: Sam Taylor <sam@finlytics.ai>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Pat O'Neill <pat@finlytics.ai>

Subject: Pilot economics — credits vs commit and quant questions

Hi Rishi / Marissa,

Thanks for the demo last week — the team was impressed with the latency profile and the cache primitives. Before we lock the pilot SOW, finance asked us to clarify two things so we can decide between a credits-based short pilot or a small committed tier:

1) Estimated unit economics: could you share an apples-to-apples comparison (per-1M token) between a credits-model pilot and a 3-month flex commit? We want to understand the break-even volume.

2) Quantization impact: our models are LoRA-adapted Llama variants (~13B). We heard Redwood recommends INT8 or 4-bit quant for production — what are the realistic accuracy tradeoffs for our prompt mix? Any guidance on when to prefer quantized variants vs running full fp16?

Attached is a short usage snapshot (Q2) and a sample prompt set. We want to size the pilot and avoid surprise quality regressions.

Primary asks: a short pricing sketch (credits vs flex commit) and a recommendation for quant options for the pilot.

Can you send a one-page that we can share with finance today?

Best,
Sam
Product Lead, Finlytics

Subject: Re: Pilot economics — credits vs commit and quant questions

Sam — thanks for the note and the snapshot, that helps a lot. High level answer up front: for a short pilot (4–6 weeks) credits give flexibility and lower upfront risk; if you expect sustained throughput beyond ~200M tokens/month we usually see commits deliver 20–30% unit-cost improvement depending on batching and cache hit rates.

I put together a one-page sketch and a recommended quant/batching approach for your prompt mix (attached) — quick summary below:

- Credits pilot: we estimate ~0.95 USD per 1k tokens effective (after expected batching and cache behavior for your Q2 mix).
- 3-month flex commit (small band): estimate ~0.70–0.80 USD per 1k tokens after reserved compute + committed discounts. Break-even at ~60–80M tokens/month.
- Quantization guidance: start pilot on 8-bit (symmetric INT8) variants for throughput testing. For the LoRA-adapted 13B models, our internal evals show negligible delta on classification/slot-filling tasks (~<1% absolute) but generation coherence can have small regressions on long-form prompts. If you need parity on long-form answers, we recommend fp16 for the first two weeks of the pilot and then parallelize the INT8 variant to validate quality vs latency/cost.

Next steps I propose:
1) We spin up a 6-week credits pilot with 50k free credits applied and performance instrumentation enabled (token-level cost, per-route latency, cache hit breakdown).
2) Simultaneous shadow runs on INT8 variants for 2 weeks to compare quality metrics on your eval prompts.
3) At week 3 we review results; if token volumes look >60M/mo we convert to a 3-month flex commit with a 15% onboarding credit.

I'll attach the one-pager and the rough numbers. Marissa — can your team prepare the pilot SOW draft (short, credits-based) so we can get signatures quickly? Karthik, any technical caveats to call out for the LoRA/INT8 path?

Thanks,
Rishi
Head of Commercials, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Pilot economics — credits vs commit and quant questions

Quick technical note from the runtime side — copying the short checklist below so Finlytics has visibility:

- INT8 path: requires a per-model calibration pass (we can run this during pilot provisioning). For LoRA adapters, calibration is low-friction but we should isolate a representative 1k-prompt set for the initial run.
- Fallbacks: enable automatic fallback policy for requests that hit a quality threshold (we can route those to fp16 transparently). This keeps customer-facing latency stable while giving you cost visibility.
- Batching: for your concurrency profile (from the snapshot) we recommend a max batch latency target of 50ms; that gives us good throughput without user-facing delay.
- Prefix/KV cache: given repeated prompt prefixes in your pipeline, we expect 10–18% additional token savings from KV caching once warmed (we'll instrument warm-up curves).

Operational ask: please confirm which model variant you want us to calibrate first (name + LoRA head). If you don't have a preference we'll pick the latest finetuned-13b-loRA-v2.

Karthik
Director, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
